description_full: Duolingo, Inc. operates as a mobile learning platform in the United States, the United Kingdom, and internationally. The company offers 250 language courses, including Spanish, English, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, Japanese, and Chinese through its Duolingo app. It also provides a digital English language proficiency assessment exam. The company was incorporated in 2011 and is headquartered in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.
ceo_bio: Dr. Luis Alfonso von Ahn Arellano Ph.D. | Co-Founder, Chairman of the Board, President & CEO | Age 46 | Compensation: $767,500 (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 900 people. Revenue per employee of $1.2M ranks in the top quartile among Technology peers, with revenue growing 43%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $411K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $153K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 1× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (8/10).
financial_summary: Duolingo, Inc. is a mid-cap technology business with a $7.8B market cap on $1.0B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +41% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +9.2pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 109% against a 10% cost of capital — a 99-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 73% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $370M in free cash flow — roughly 36 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.94× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 40× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and stock-based comp at 13% of revenue is silent dilution an owner has to account for, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.
